frontmatter.title: Project: Ocean Only Configuration - The Bare Minimum

children.value: This project is all about how we create the most basic ocean_only domain to shake things out, get spinning as fast as possible. Test everything before we get into our research question.
Download this project by either:
Running the CrocoDash CLI command:
crocodash template --machine derecho --notebook crocodash.projects.ocean_only
Copying the file from your CrocoDash checkout:
demos/crocodash/projects/ocean_only
Grid Generation - The first thing we are going to do is think about how to get a fast domain going, so I might look at some scaling data we’ve put online:
https://​crocodile​-cesm​.github​.io​/SeaSloth​/mom6​_scaling​.html
Given how fast a 100x100 domain is, I think we should go with that, with maybe 40 cores for the Ocean. That’ll run wicked fast.
We’ll pick an arbitrary vertical grid.

from CrocoDash.grid import Grid
from CrocoDash.vgrid import VGrid

grid = Grid(
  resolution = 0.05, # in degrees
  xstart = 278.0, # min longitude in [0, 360]
  lenx = 5.0, # longitude extent in degrees
  ystart = 7.0, # min latitude in [-90, 90]
  leny = 5.0, # latitude extent in degrees
  name = "basic_grid",
)


vgrid  = VGrid.hyperbolic(
    nk = 75, # number of vertical levels
    depth = 2000,
    ratio=20.0 # target ratio of top to bottom layer thicknesses
)
Now that we have our grids, we need to setup a bathymetry object. Normally, we’d use the
Topo.set_from_dataset
function to go from “obs” to a bathymetry on our grid. But we’re trying to move with purpose, so we can use some Topo functions to create our own fun little domain.

from CrocoDash.topo import Topo

topo = Topo(
    grid = grid,
    min_depth = 9.5, # in meters
)

topo.set_bowl(max_depth = 2000, dedge = 200)

topo.depth.plot()
Great! So I’m going to create my case now, and this step will hardly every change

from pathlib import Path
from CrocoDash.case import Case

# CESM case (experiment) name

# CESM source root (Update this path accordingly!!!)

# CESM case directory

case = Case(
    cesmroot = cesmroot,
    caseroot = caseroot,
    inputdir = inputdir,
    ocn_grid = grid,
    ocn_vgrid = vgrid,
    ocn_topo = topo,
    project = "<PROJECT>", # Update this with your project code
    override = True,
    machine = "derecho",
    compset = "CR_JRA"
)

children.value: Now, the last step is to generate forcings. Which we do with a configure and process step. It always takes a long time to get raw data from other places, so we’re going to use a fake data product. I also think we can run for 60 days. Doesn’t sound too bad.

case.configure_forcings(
    date_range = ["2019-01-01 00:00:00", "2019-03-03 00:00:00"],
    product_name="reference_ocean",
    function_name="get_reference_ocean_data"
)
case.process_forcings()
Cool! Once this is done we have to
case.build
and
case.submit
in our case directory. Before that though, here’s some things I’d
xmlchange
to run faster.
I’d set the NTASKS=10, which sets every component to 10 cores, and makes the data atmosphere regridding very fast. (All components share these 10 cores)
I’d set the NTASKS_OCN=40 because of the scaling data we saw.
I’d set the ROOTPE=0, which ensures that all components share the same cores. If I set ROOTPE_OCN=10, it would skip the first 10 cores and run on the next 40 cores.
I’d set the JOB_WALLCLOCK_TIME=00:30:00 --subgroup
case.run
, which ensures the queue picks up our job realllly fast.
And there we go! A fake running ocean model! Isn’t that awesome!
